rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient to test whether its substantial resolution margin permits a faster fully resolved separation.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the resolution boundary for the critical middle pair. The 8-minute gradient remains a proven maximum-CRF fallback if this compression reduces resolution below 1.5.

Test whether higher temperature shifts selectivity enough to resolve the critical middle pair at the faster gradient. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect, with injection 2 retained as the fully resolved fallback.

Use an intermediate temperature to avoid the early-pair coelution seen at 60 C, and reduce gradient steepness to improve the critical middle separation. This tests a potentially faster maximum-CRF method while keeping the final organic fraction above the observed elution window.

Raise the gradient window while preserving the slope and temperature of injection 5 to reduce elution times. The new starting fraction remains below the estimated first-peak elution fraction, but this run will check whether early retention and critical-pair resolution remain sufficient.
Slightly reduce gradient steepness to recover the small resolution deficit in injection 6. Keeping its higher starting fraction should preserve most of the time saving over injection 5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness to protect the critical middle pair. Check that the early pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved.

Test a narrower, higher-starting window to bring the last peak forward while using a shallower slope to protect the middle pair. This also probes the starting-organic limit for resolving the first two peaks.

Increase the endpoint one step to shorten the separation while testing the remaining resolution margin in injection 9. Keep the starting fraction and temperature unchanged because the early pair is approaching its resolution limit.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a distinct fast-gradient regime: stronger compression may reverse the critical middle pair and restore its separation. Lower temperature may protect the early pair, which became poorly resolved at high temperature.

Probe whether a higher starting fraction strengthens separation of the reordered middle pair in the fast-gradient regime. A moderate temperature increase may improve the late pair while retaining more early-pair selectivity than at 50–60 C.

Test whether a higher starting fraction improves the reordered middle-pair separation, using low temperature to preserve early retention. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 8 as the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Return to the fully resolved selectivity regime of injection 8, trimming the endpoint and shortening the programmed gradient to four minutes. The slightly steeper slope tests whether a faster separation can retain the critical pair's resolution.

Increase the starting fraction one step from injection 13 to test whether differential retention widens its critical middle pair enough for full resolution. This is a deliberate boundary test: the first peak may be essentially unretained, but the early pair previously had substantial separation.

Lower the endpoint at the same starting fraction and temperature to test how the reordered middle pair responds to a shallower gradient. The late peaks previously eluted near 0.65 organic, so a short final hold should allow complete elution without truncation.

Further reduce gradient steepness to build on the middle-pair improvement from injection 16. The lower endpoint will delay the last peak into the hold, but may deliver full resolution with a shorter separation than the established maximum-CRF methods.

Use a slope midway between injections 9 and 10 to target full resolution with a last peak near 3.4 minutes. This returns to a proven selectivity region and trims the programmed gradient to four minutes without placing the final peak in the hold.

Lower temperature one step from injection 18 to measure local selectivity changes without changing the gradient. Improved early-pair separation could permit a higher starting fraction, provided the critical middle pair remains resolved.

Use the extra early-pair resolution at 45 C to test a higher starting fraction, while making the gradient shallower to protect the middle pair. This probes whether shifting and narrowing the elution window can preserve maximum CRF with earlier elution.

Back away from the high-starting-organic boundary and slightly reduce steepness relative to injection 14 to restore full resolution. This targets a short maximum-CRF method with more resolution margin than injection 18.

Test the remaining intermediate temperature with a lower starting fraction and shallower slope to protect the early pair. This checks whether 55 C can retain full resolution without the selectivity collapse observed at 60 C.

Return to 50 C and use a slightly shallower slope than injection 21 to increase the critical-pair resolution margin. This targets a robust maximum-CRF alternative while retaining injection 18 as the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Test a one-step temperature reduction from injection 21 to improve early-pair separation while using its middle-pair resolution margin. This targets a balanced, fully resolved alternative; injection 18 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to reduce steepness one step from injection 18, targeting greater critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the separation short. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.
